findings.title: Federated recovery codes can be reused indefinitely
findings.body: The new `isValid` implementation for `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE` only checks whether the supplied input matches any of the originally generated codes in `getCredentialData()`, but never updates the credential data or any other state to mark a code as consumed. As a result, once a recovery code is written into the federated store it can be submitted over and over and `isValid` will keep returning `true`. Recovery codes must be single-use; the local `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider` mutates its credential data on each successful `isValid` call, so the contract that the federated provider now implements must do the same (e.g. by calling `updateCredential` to remove the consumed code). Without this, the feature quietly downgrades from one-time codes to reusable passwords for any user coming from a federated storage that adopts this PR.

findings.title: Federated recovery-code model never reports `allCodesUsed()`
findings.body: `getCredentials` reconstructs the `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel` via `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues(...)` from the full original code list stored in `credentialData`, and it never updates `credentialData` after `isValid` succeeds (see the other finding). Because the storage doesn't track consumption, `recoveryCodeCredentialModel.allCodesUsed()` in `RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator` will always be `false` for federated users, so the credential is never removed and the `CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES` required action is never added even after the user has burned through every code. The credential data must be mutated on each successful validation (consumed code removed) for `allCodesUsed()` and the single-use semantics to work.

findings.title: Federated recovery codes cannot be removed after use
findings.body: After a successful verification, the authenticator calls `authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(recoveryCodeCredentialModel.getId())` whenever `allCodesUsed()` returns true. `removeStoredCredentialById` only operates on local (Keycloak DB) credentials. With this PR, `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(...)` now returns federated credentials as well, so when the federated store reports all codes consumed the call silently does nothing and the user is left with an empty/unusable credential. The code needs to use the credential-manager path appropriate for federated credentials (e.g. `removeCredential` / delegating to the user-storage provider), or branch on whether the credential is federated vs. stored.

findings.title: `getCredentials` returns recovery-code credential with a fresh, non-matching ID
findings.body: `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues(...)` is called without forwarding the stored `CredentialModel.id`. The credential returned to Keycloak therefore has a brand-new id, which means any later operation that uses that id (e.g. deletion via the account REST endpoint, or any internal code that persists the recovered model) will target a different record than what is actually stored. The `MyUser.recoveryCodes` `id` (set in `updateCredential` via `KeycloakModelUtils.generateId()`) must be propagated to the returned model so that id-based lookups and removals line up.

findings.title: Return value of local `createCredential` is ignored
findings.body: `createRecoveryCodesCredential` checks the boolean returned by `user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...)` but discards the result of `recoveryCodeCredentialProvider.createCredential(realm, user, credentialModel)`. If local creation fails (e.g. DB constraint violation, provider exception), the method returns normally and the caller in `RecoveryAuthnCodesAction.processAction` then calls `reqActionContext.success()` even though no credential was actually stored. Either propagate the failure (throw, or return a boolean) or at minimum log an error; `createOTPCredential` directly above for comparison returns a boolean for the same reason.

findings.title: Login bean throws `NoSuchElementException` when no recovery credential exists
findings.body: The constructor calls `credentialModelOpt.get()` without checking presence. Because `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential` now consults federated storage first and then local storage, any user that legitimately has no recovery codes configured will cause this bean (and therefore the login form rendering it) to throw an unchecked `NoSuchElementException`. The pre-existing code already had the same `.get()` on `findFirst()`, but since the change introduces a new lookup path that crosses storage boundaries the failure surface expands. Guard with `ifPresent`/`orElseThrow` that produces a meaningful message, or have the template skip the prompt entirely when there is no credential.

findings.title: Recovery-codes test never asserts codes are single-use
findings.body: `testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin` only exercises a successful login with the first requested code. It does not (a) verify the same code cannot be reused on a second login, (b) verify that `allCodesUsed()` flips after consuming every code, (c) verify that the credential is removed from user storage once exhausted, or (d) verify that `CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES` becomes a required action afterwards. Given the federated-storage bugs reported above (no consumption tracking, `removeStoredCredentialById` is wrong API, id mismatch), these are exactly the cases that would catch them. The test currently passes only because it never asks the user-storage provider to mutate state.

findings.title: `getCredential` shadows a different lookup semantic from the old call site
findings.body: `getCredential` returns the first federated credential that matches the type, with no fallback if a local credential also exists. In the (admittedly rare) situation where both a federated and a local `recovery-authn-codes` credential coexist for the same user, the local one is silently ignored. This is a behaviour change vs. the previous code in `RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator` and `RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean`, which only ever looked at local storage. Worth either documenting the precedence rule explicitly in the javadoc or merging both sources with a deterministic ordering.
